sentences.text: Thoracosaurus was a long-snouted eusuchian crocodilian.
The European form T. scanicus was a relatively large gavialoid with a body length of over 4.4 meters and a skull 55 centimeters long.
The genus Thoracosaurus was first described by Leidy in 1852.
A redescription and study on the affinities of T. isorhynchus was published by Boerman et al. in 2026.
Thoracosaurus is thought to have lived in marine environments.
There are 53 recorded fossil occurrences of Thoracosaurus.
Thoracosaurus belongs to the superfamily Gavialoidea.
The parent group of Thoracosaurus is the family Gavialidae.
Research beginning in the 1990s placed Thoracosaurus within Gavialoidea, excluding modern false gharials.
The type species for the genus Thoracosaurus is T. neocesariensis.
The genus includes the type species T. neocesariensis from North America and T. isorhynchus or T. macrorhynchus from Europe.
A recent review argues that T. macrorhynchus is a junior synonym of T. isorhynchus.
If European and North American forms cannot be differentiated, T. isorhynchus would be considered a nomen dubium.
Many species have been assigned to Thoracosaurus, but most are considered dubious.
The genus includes the type species T. neocesariensis, as well as T. macrorhynchus and T. scanicus.
The genus authority for Thoracosaurus is Leidy, 1852.
Thoracosaurus fossils date from the Late Cretaceous to the Early Paleocene.
This extinct genus, known as the chest lizard, lived in North America and Europe during the Late Cretaceous and Early Paleocene.
Thoracosaurus was an extinct gavialoid crocodilian that lived during the Late Cretaceous and the beginning of the Paleocene.
The time range for Thoracosaurus is from the Santonian to the Ypresian, between 85.7 and 48.07 million years ago.
A 2018 study suggests Thoracosaurus might have been a non-crocodylian eusuchian, though this is debated.
